course.title: Darwin's Natural Selection: Reading Chapter IV of On the Origin of Species
course.description: A close reading of the opening pages of Chapter IV of Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859), in which Darwin defines natural selection, contrasts it with selection practiced by human breeders, and shows how even seemingly trivial characters can be shaped by it. Each lesson stays anchored to Darwin's own arguments, examples, and language in the excerpt.

lessons.title: The Question Darwin Sets Himself
lessons.content:
# The Question Darwin Sets Himself

## A chapter that opens with a table of contents

Victorian scientific books often prefaced each chapter with a compressed summary heading — a list of the topics to come, in order. Chapter IV of *On the Origin of Species* begins with one, and it is worth reading slowly, because it is Darwin's own map of the argument:

> Natural Selection: its power compared with man's selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes. Sexual Selection. On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species. Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals. Slow action. Extinction caused by Natural Selection. Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation. Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent. Explains the Grouping of all organic beings.

Notice the trajectory. The chapter begins with a comparison — nature's selection set beside the breeder's — and ends with a claim of enormous scope: that this one principle *explains the grouping of all organic beings*, the whole nested arrangement of life into species, genera, families. In between come the sub-topics: sexual selection, intercrossing, isolation, population size, slowness of action, extinction, and divergence of character. The heading tells you in advance that Darwin does not intend to stop at "animals change a bit." He is heading for taxonomy itself.

## The opening question

The chapter proper opens with two questions and an answer:

> How will the struggle for existence, discussed too briefly in the last chapter, act in regard to variation? Can the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature? I think we shall see that it can act most effectually.

Everything hangs on the word *act*. Darwin is not asking whether organisms vary — he has already argued that they do. He is not asking whether more individuals are born than can survive — that was the previous chapter. He is asking what happens when you put those two facts together: what does a struggle for existence *do* to a pool of variation?

The second question is a transfer question. In the earlier chapters Darwin had shown breeders producing pigeons, dogs, and cabbages of astonishing diversity by picking which individuals reproduce. Can that same principle operate where there is no picker? The rest of the chapter is the answer.

## The premises he asks you to bear in mind

Before arguing, Darwin lays out what the reader should hold in mind. He repeats the phrase "let it be borne in mind" like a refrain:

1. **The extent of variation.** Domestic productions vary in "an endless number of strange peculiarities," and wild ones do too, though "in a lesser degree." Note the asymmetry: he does not claim nature varies as freely as the farmyard.
2. **The strength of heredity.** Variation would be useless to selection if offspring did not resemble parents; Darwin insists "how strong the hereditary tendency is." Under domestication, he adds, "the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic."
3. **The complexity of relations.** The mutual relations of organic beings to each other and to their physical conditions are "infinitely complex and close-fitting." This matters because it means there are countless ways a slight change could help — or hurt.

From these he builds a short chain of rhetorical questions. Variations useful *to man* have undoubtedly occurred; is it improbable that variations useful *to the being itself*, in the "great and complex battle of life," should sometimes occur over thousands of generations? And if they do occur — remembering that many more individuals are born than can survive — can we doubt that an individual with any advantage, "however slight," would have the best chance of surviving and leaving offspring? Meanwhile any variation "in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

## The definition

Then comes the naming sentence:

> This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.

Two things deserve emphasis. First, the definition is two-sided: preservation *and* rejection. It is not merely that good things are kept; bad things are eliminated. Second, the definition names a *process*, not an agent or a force. Darwin defines natural selection as the preservation-and-rejection itself.

## The third category: neither useful nor injurious

Immediately after defining the term, Darwin adds a qualification that readers often skip:

> Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.

This is a real limit on the theory, stated by its author on the page where he introduces it. Natural selection has no grip on a variation that makes no difference to survival. Such variations simply fluctuate — and Darwin suggests the polymorphic species, those existing in several stable forms at once, may be examples.

It is worth putting this alongside a later passage in the chapter, where Darwin insists that characters we consider trifling — the down on a fruit, the colour of a grouse — often turn out to matter after all. There is no contradiction. His point there is that we are poor judges of what is useful; his point here is that whatever is genuinely useless is genuinely outside selection's reach.

## Why frame it as a question at all?

Darwin could have opened with a declaration. Instead he opens by asking whether his own analogy holds. This is a deliberate rhetorical strategy for a book addressed to sceptics: he raises the doubt himself, in the reader's voice, and then answers it. The whole of Chapter IV is structured as the working-out of an answer to a question posed in the first two sentences — and the summary heading has already told you that the answer reaches all the way to the grouping of all organic beings.

### A note on "however slight"

Keep an eye on this phrase. Darwin's argument does not require dramatic mutations or monstrous births. It requires only that some individuals have *any* advantage, however slight, and that many more are born than can survive. The slightness is essential to the argument, not a weakness in it — it is what allows the process to work on ordinary, everyday differences rather than waiting for rarities.

lessons.content:
# Preservation and Rejection: The Definition

Chapter III of the *Origin* left Darwin with a problem he states plainly at the opening of Chapter IV:

> How will the struggle for existence, discussed too briefly in the last chapter, act in regard to variation? Can the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature?

His answer — "I think we shall see that it can act most effectually" — is not asserted but argued for. What follows is a short chain of premises, each of which Darwin has already established earlier in the book, assembled here into a definition. It is worth walking the chain link by link, because the famous definition at the end is only as strong as the steps leading to it.

## Link 1: Organisation is plastic

Darwin first asks the reader to "bear in mind in what an endless number of strange peculiarities our domestic productions, and, in a lesser degree, those under nature, vary." Note the comparison: variation is *greater* under domestication, but it is not confined there. Wild forms vary too, only less floridly.

His summary phrase for the domestic case is striking: "Under domestication, it may be truly said that the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic." Not just a feather here or a bone there — the whole organisation. If the raw material of change is that abundant, then the question is no longer *whether* new forms can appear but what will happen to them once they do.

## Link 2: Heredity is strong

Variation alone would be useless if offspring reverted to the parental type. Darwin therefore couples the plasticity claim immediately with "how strong the hereditary tendency is." A favourable peculiarity that could not be handed on would die with its possessor and leave nature exactly where she started.

## Link 3: The relations of organic beings are complex and close-fitting

> Let it be borne in mind how infinitely complex and close-fitting are the mutual relations of all organic beings to each other and to their physical conditions of life.

This link does two jobs. First, it means there are many, many ways for a being to be slightly better or slightly worse off — the surface of contact between an organism and its world is enormous, so there are countless dimensions along which a variation might matter. Second, because relations are *close-fitting*, small changes are not swallowed up as noise; they press somewhere.

## Link 4: The argument by analogy from man

Having set those three facts down, Darwin asks his rhetorical question:

> Can it, then, be thought improbable, seeing that variations useful to man have undoubtedly occurred, that other variations useful in some way to each being in the great and complex battle of life, should sometimes occur in the course of thousands of generations?

The logic is that of a lesser to a greater case. Variations useful to *human purposes* — longer wool, fatter breasts of meat, a fancier pigeon — are an undoubted fact of the breeder's yard. Those purposes are narrow and arbitrary. Why should variations useful to the animal's *own* business of living be rarer? And the time available is not one breeder's lifetime but "thousands of generations."

## Link 5: More are born than can survive

The last link is the Malthusian one, and Darwin puts it in a parenthesis as something already agreed:

> If such do occur, can we doubt (remembering that many more individuals are born than can possibly survive) that individuals having any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind?

This is what converts a mere difference into a consequence. If every individual born survived and bred, an advantage would be a curiosity. Because most must die, an advantage — "however slight" — becomes a better chance of being among the survivors. And survival is not the point either: Darwin says surviving *and procreating their kind*, since it is the transmitted variation that matters.

The negative half follows at once: "we may feel sure that any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

## The definition

> This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.

Two halves, then, not one. Preservation *and* rejection. It is easy to remember natural selection as a machine for keeping good things and forget that the destroying half is doing equal work.

Notice also what the definition does *not* claim. It says nothing about a purpose, a designer, or a goal; it is simply the name Darwin gives to a consequence of the five facts above. In a later passage he restates the same thing as an ongoing process rather than a rule: natural selection "is daily and hourly scrutinising, throughout the world, every variation, even the slightest; rejecting that which is bad, preserving and adding up all that is good; silently and insensibly working, whenever and wherever opportunity offers." *Adding up* is important — the process is cumulative, not a single sieving.

## The third category: neutral variations

Darwin adds a qualification that is often dropped when the definition is quoted:

> Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.

So variations fall into three classes, not two: favourable (preserved), injurious (rejected), and neutral (untouched). Selection has no grip on the third class, which is therefore free to fluctuate. Darwin's suggested evidence is polymorphic species — those that persist with several forms at once, as if nothing were choosing between them.

This is an honest limit on the theory, and it matters. Natural selection is not offered as an explanation of *every* character; it explains those characters that make a difference to survival.

## "However slight" — a caution

One further point guards against a misreading. Because Darwin says the definition covers even trifling advantages, he is committed to the view that apparently insignificant characters can be selected. He defends this elsewhere in the chapter with examples: leaf-eating insects are green and bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan is white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather. Hawks hunt by eyesight, so much so "that on parts of the Continent persons are warned not to keep white pigeons, as being the most liable to destruction." Colour looks like a trifle; to a grouse it is not. What counts as favourable is decided by the close-fitting relations of Link 3, not by what strikes a human observer as important.

## Summary of the chain

1. Organisation is plastic — variation is abundant, especially under domestication but also in nature.
2. The hereditary tendency is strong — variations can be passed on.
3. Relations among organic beings are complex and close-fitting — small differences have somewhere to bite.
4. Variations useful to man demonstrably occur; over thousands of generations, variations useful to the being itself should occur too.
5. Many more individuals are born than can possibly survive — so any advantage, however slight, gives the best chance of surviving and procreating.

∴ Favourable variations are preserved, injurious ones rigidly destroyed. **This is natural selection.** Neutral variations are left to fluctuate.

lessons.title: Variations That Are Neither Useful Nor Injurious
lessons.content:
# Variations That Are Neither Useful Nor Injurious

## The sentence that limits the principle

After Darwin defines his central mechanism, he immediately adds a qualification that is easy to read past. Here is the definition and the qualification together:

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection. Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

Notice the structure of the claim. Natural selection is defined by two operations, not one:

1. **Preservation** of variations that give an advantage, "however slight."
2. **Rejection** of variations "in the least degree injurious," which Darwin says would be "rigidly destroyed."

Both operations require the variation to *matter* to the being's chances in the struggle for life. A variation that helps nothing and harms nothing gives selection no purchase. There is no third operation for the indifferent case. Such variations are simply left alone.

## "A fluctuating element"

The phrase Darwin chooses is precise. He does not say that neutral variations disappear, nor that they are preserved. He says they are **left a fluctuating element** — free to drift up and down in a population because nothing is pushing them in either direction. Where selection is at work, Darwin expects character to be made "true and constant" (his phrase for what selection does to the colour of a grouse once acquired). Where selection has nothing to grip, we should expect the opposite: variability that persists rather than settling down.

His suggested illustration is the group of species naturalists call **polymorphic** — species that occur in several distinct forms at once. Darwin's wording is careful here too: "as *perhaps* we see in the species called polymorphic." He offers it as a likely instance, not a demonstration.

## A second limit: selection needs something to work with

The neutrality qualification is not the only boundary Darwin draws around his own principle. Later in the same chapter he states another, just as flatly:

> "unless profitable variations do occur, natural selection can do nothing."

This is why he treats a change in the conditions of life as *favourable* to natural selection: by acting on the reproductive system it "causes or increases variability," and so gives "a better chance of profitable variations occurring." Selection is not a creative force that summons up what is needed; it is a sieve, and a sieve does nothing if nothing is poured through it.

A third limit follows from the definition itself: selection "can act only through and for the good of each being." It has no other criterion. As Darwin puts it in contrasting nature with the human breeder, "nature cares nothing for appearances, except in so far as they may be useful to any being."

## How hard it is to know what is neutral

Having granted that some variations escape selection, Darwin spends the following pages warning us not to be too quick in deciding which ones those are. Characters "which we are apt to consider as of very trifling importance" often turn out to matter:

- Leaf-eating insects are green, bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan is white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, the black-grouse that of peaty earth. Grouse suffer largely from birds of prey, and "hawks are guided by eyesight to their prey" — so much so that on parts of the Continent people are warned not to keep white pigeons, as the most liable to destruction.
- Botanists rank the down on a fruit and the colour of its flesh among "characters of the most trifling importance." Yet the horticulturist Downing reports that in the United States smooth-skinned fruits suffer far more from a beetle, the curculio, than downy ones; that purple plums suffer far more from a certain disease than yellow plums; and that another disease attacks yellow-fleshed peaches more than other-fleshed ones.

Darwin's point is that if such differences "make a great difference" even under cultivation, with all the aids of art, then in a state of nature they "would effectually settle which variety" succeeds. And he adds the memorable domestic comparison: we should remember "how essential it is in a flock of white sheep to destroy every lamb with the faintest trace of black" — the occasional destruction of animals of one colour is not a negligible thing.

## Reading the qualification correctly

So the lesson cuts two ways at once.

- **Against over-reach:** natural selection is not a universal explanation for every feature of an organism. Darwin himself carves out the class of indifferent variations and hands them to something else — fluctuation.
- **Against over-use of that escape clause:** "neither useful nor injurious" is a real category, but a naturalist's confidence that a given character belongs to it is worth little. Down, flesh colour, and plumage tint all looked trifling and were not.

The honest position Darwin models is this: state the mechanism, state where it does not apply, and then be slow to assume any particular case falls in the exempt class.

lessons.content:
# A Country Undergoing Physical Change

Having defined natural selection — "this preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations" — Darwin needs a way to show it *working*. He does not begin with a fossil, or an experiment, or a statistic. He begins with a thought experiment:

> "We shall best understand the probable course of natural selection by taking the case of a country undergoing some physical change, for instance, of climate."

The whole rest of the chapter's argument grows out of this imagined country. It is worth walking through it slowly, because Darwin packs several distinct claims into a few sentences.

## Step one: the proportions shift at once

Suppose the climate of some country alters — it grows colder, or drier, or the seasons lengthen. What follows?

> "The proportional numbers of its inhabitants would almost immediately undergo a change, and some species might become extinct."

Notice what Darwin emphasises. The first and quickest effect is not the appearance of new forms, nor even extinction; it is a change in *proportions*. Species that were common become scarce; scarce ones become common. Extinction is mentioned second, and hedged — "some species **might** become extinct." The immediate, guaranteed consequence is a re-shuffling of relative numbers.

## Step two: the knock-on effects, independent of the climate

This is the subtle and important move. Darwin appeals back to what he has already established about how tightly the inhabitants of a country are bound to one another:

> "We may conclude, from what we have seen of the intimate and complex manner in which the inhabitants of each country are bound together, that any change in the numerical proportions of some of the inhabitants, **independently of the change of climate itself**, would most seriously affect many of the others."

Read that italicised phrase carefully. Darwin is separating two kinds of pressure:

1. **The direct effect of the climate** — a species that cannot tolerate the new cold declines because of the cold.
2. **The indirect effect of altered numbers** — a species perfectly comfortable in the new climate declines anyway, because the insect it depends on has grown scarce, or the herbivore that used to crop its competitors has multiplied.

The second kind of pressure would exist even if the climate had never touched those particular species. In an earlier chapter Darwin has described the relations among organisms as "infinitely complex and close-fitting"; here that complexity becomes a transmission mechanism. Push one part of the web and the shock travels far beyond where the hand fell. A change in climate is therefore not one cause of change but the first of a long chain, most of whose links are organic rather than physical.

## Step three: if the borders are open

Darwin then adds a further disturbance:

> "If the country were open on its borders, new forms would certainly immigrate, and this also would seriously disturb the relations of some of the former inhabitants."

Again the pressure is relational. The immigrants do not need to be climatic specialists; they simply need to compete, eat, or be eaten, and the old balance is unsettled.

And here Darwin reaches for his one piece of hard evidence in the passage:

> "Let it be remembered how powerful the influence of a single introduced tree or mammal has been shown to be."

The word to underline is *single*. The claim is not that mass invasion transforms a country — that would surprise nobody. It is that **one** species, one tree or one mammal, has been *demonstrated* to reorganise the life of a region. Darwin is not speculating; he is calling on cases already "shown" (in his earlier chapter he had described how a single kind of Scotch fir, once fenced from cattle, transformed a heath, bringing with it different insects and different insect-eating birds). If one introduction can do that much, then the far larger re-shuffling caused by a change of climate must be enormous.

## Why this matters for the argument

The thought experiment does two jobs at once.

First, it manufactures **opportunity**. Once proportions shift, species vanish, and relations are disturbed, there are gaps — Darwin will call them "places in the economy of nature" — that could be better filled than they currently are. Where a country is open, immigrants seize those places. Where it is closed, as on an island, the only way for the places to be better filled is for some of the original inhabitants to be modified, and every slight modification that better fits them to the altered conditions tends to be preserved.

Second, it supplies **raw material**. Darwin has argued in his first chapter that changed conditions of life, by acting specially on the reproductive system, cause or increase variability. So the very event that opens the gaps also improves the chances that profitable variations will occur — "and unless profitable variations do occur, natural selection can do nothing."

## A caution Darwin himself adds

Having built the scenario, he immediately insists it is not required:

> "Nor do I believe that any great physical change, as of climate, or any unusual degree of isolation to check immigration, is actually necessary..."

The climate shift is a teaching device — a way of making visible, in one dramatic stroke, a process that ordinarily proceeds unseen. Because all the inhabitants of a country are "struggling together with nicely balanced forces," even extremely slight modifications can tip the balance without any grand physical upheaval at all. The changing country is the loud version of something that is always happening quietly.

lessons.title: Open Borders, Islands, and Places in the Economy of Nature
lessons.content:
# Open Borders, Islands, and Places in the Economy of Nature

## A thought experiment about climate

Darwin wants to show natural selection actually *working*, not merely assert that it could. So he sets up a scenario: "We shall best understand the probable course of natural selection by taking the case of a country undergoing some physical change, for instance, of climate."

What happens first? Not extinction of the unfit in some dramatic sense, but a shift in numbers. "The proportional numbers of its inhabitants would almost immediately undergo a change, and some species might become extinct." And because the inhabitants of a country are bound together in an "intimate and complex manner," a change in the numerical proportions of a few species — quite apart from the climate change itself — would "most seriously affect many of the others."

So the climate shift is only the first push. The real disturbance ripples outward through the web of relations.

## The fork in the road: open border or barrier?

Now Darwin splits the scenario in two, and this split is the heart of the passage.

**Case 1: the country is open on its borders.** Then "new forms would certainly immigrate, and this also would seriously disturb the relations of some of the former inhabitants." Darwin reminds us how much damage a *single* introduced tree or mammal has been shown to do. The disturbance is real and profound — but notice what it does *not* do. Immigration fills the gaps with ready-made occupants. Nothing native has to change.

**Case 2: an island, or a country partly surrounded by barriers,** "into which new and better adapted forms could not freely enter." Here the same gaps open up, but nothing arrives to plug them. In Darwin's phrase, "we should then have places in the economy of nature which would assuredly be better filled up, if some of the original inhabitants were in some manner modified; for, had the area been open to immigration, these same places would have been seized on by intruders."

## What is a "place in the economy of nature"?

The metaphor is economic and it is worth pausing on. A "place" is a way of making a living — a role in the local economy of eating, being eaten, competing, and reproducing. When conditions shift, some places are vacated and new ones open. Such a place can be filled in exactly two ways:

1. **By an immigrant** already adapted to something like it, arriving from outside.
2. **By a resident**, slowly modified until it fits.

Route 1 is fast; route 2 is slow. Where both are available, the fast route wins and the slow one never gets started. Isolation matters not because it creates opportunity, but because it *protects* opportunity from being taken by the quicker route.

Under those conditions, Darwin writes, "every slight modification, which in the course of ages chanced to arise, and which in any way favoured the individuals of any of the species, by better adapting them to their altered conditions, would tend to be preserved; and natural selection would thus have free scope for the work of improvement."

"Free scope" is precise. Selection is not made *stronger* by the barrier. It is simply left unobstructed.

## The change in conditions helps twice over

There is a second benefit hidden in the setup. Darwin has argued earlier that "a change in the conditions of life, by specially acting on the reproductive system, causes or increases variability." So the altered climate both opens the places *and* raises the supply of raw material — "giving a better chance of profitable variations occurring; and unless profitable variations do occur, natural selection can do nothing."

That last clause is a genuine limit on the theory. Selection is a filter, not a generator. With no variations to sift, it is idle.

But Darwin immediately guards against overstating the need: no "extreme amount of variability is necessary." Man gets great results by adding up mere individual differences; Nature can do the same "far more easily, from having incomparably longer time at her disposal."

## The retraction: none of this is actually required

Having built the island scenario carefully, Darwin then takes much of it back — and this is easy to miss on a first reading. He does *not* believe "that any great physical change, as of climate, or any unusual degree of isolation to check immigration, is actually necessary to produce new and unoccupied places for natural selection to fill up."

Why not? Because of the phrase "nicely balanced forces." All the inhabitants of a country are struggling together, and the balance is fine enough that "extremely slight modifications in the structure or habits of one inhabitant would often give it an advantage over others; and still further modifications of the same kind would often still further increase the advantage."

The island is therefore best read as a **clarifying** case, not a **necessary** one. It strips away the confounding factor of immigration so we can watch the mechanism plainly. In the messier real world, the mechanism runs anyway.

## The naturalisation argument

Darwin closes the argument with a piece of evidence anyone can check. Someone might object: perhaps the natives of a country are already perfect, leaving no room for improvement. He answers:

> "No country can be named in which all the native inhabitants are now so perfectly adapted to each other and to the physical conditions under which they live, that none of them could anyhow be improved; for in all countries, the natives have been so far conquered by naturalised productions, that they have allowed foreigners to take firm possession of the land."

The logic runs: foreign species have successfully established themselves *everywhere*. If natives were unimprovable, no foreigner could have found a foothold. "And as foreigners have thus everywhere beaten some of the natives, we may safely conclude that the natives might have been modified with advantage, so as to have better resisted such intruders."

Naturalisation is thus turned into a global demonstration that vacant or improvable places exist in every country on earth.

## Summary of the chain

- Physical change → shift in numbers → ripple through the web of relations → open places.
- Open border → intruders seize the places → residents unchanged.
- Barrier → places persist unfilled → slight favourable variations preserved → "free scope for the work of improvement."
- But: nicely balanced forces mean places open even without barriers or climate change.
- Proof that places exist everywhere: foreigners have taken firm possession of land in every country.

lessons.title: Variability, Time, and the Test of Naturalised Productions
lessons.content:
# Variability, Time, and the Test of Naturalised Productions

Natural selection has one absolute precondition. Darwin states it flatly: "unless profitable variations do occur, natural selection can do nothing." Selection is a sieve, not a fountain — it can preserve and accumulate, but it cannot conjure the raw material it works on. So the obvious next question is: where does that raw material come from, and how much of it do we need?

This lesson follows Darwin's answer through three moves: a source of variation, a pair of denials about what is *not* necessary, and finally an empirical test that shows there is always room for improvement.

## 1. Changed conditions and the reproductive system

Darwin's stated source of increased variability is a change in the conditions of life:

> "We have reason to believe, as stated in the first chapter, that a change in the conditions of life, by specially acting on the reproductive system, causes or increases variability."

Note the mechanism he proposes. The changed conditions do not directly mould the adult body into a useful new shape. They act **on the reproductive system**, and the result is that offspring vary more. The variation is thrown up; whether it is useful is settled afterwards, by the struggle for life.

This is why Darwin's worked example in this chapter begins with a country undergoing a physical change such as a change of climate. Such a change does double duty. It reshuffles the numerical proportions of the inhabitants and opens up places in the economy of nature — and, by altering the conditions of life, it also raises the supply of variation. As Darwin puts it, this "would manifestly be favourable to natural selection, by giving a better chance of profitable variations occurring."

## 2. Two things Darwin insists are *not* necessary

Having described a favourable case, Darwin immediately guards against the reader over-reading it. He makes two denials.

**(a) No extreme amount of variability is necessary.** The comparison is with the breeder:

> "as man can certainly produce great results by adding up in any given direction mere individual differences, so could Nature, but far more easily, from having incomparably longer time at her disposal."

The breeder does not wait for monsters; he takes the small individual differences that are always present and adds them up in one direction. Nature can do the same. And Nature's advantage in this comparison is explicitly **time**, not superior material. Man's efforts are fleeting and his life short; nature accumulates "during whole geological periods." Slight differences plus enormous time substitute for dramatic variation.

**(b) No great physical change or unusual isolation is necessary either.** Darwin denies that a climatic upheaval, or barriers checking immigration, are actually required to open up "new and unoccupied places" for selection to fill. His reason is the balance of the existing community:

> "as all the inhabitants of each country are struggling together with nicely balanced forces, extremely slight modifications in the structure or habits of one inhabitant would often give it an advantage over others; and still further modifications of the same kind would often still further increase the advantage."

Because the forces are *nicely balanced*, a very small push tips the scale. And the advantage compounds: once a modification pays, more of the same pays more. The opportunity for selection is therefore permanent, built into the crowded, interlocking relations of any community, rather than something that arrives only with a geological crisis.

Be careful about what the denials do and do not say. Changed conditions are *favourable* to natural selection; they are not its prerequisite. The prerequisite is only that profitable variations occur.

## 3. The test: naturalised productions

A sceptic might reply that a long-established native fauna and flora may simply have finished the job — that its members are already as well fitted to one another and to their climate as anything could be, leaving nothing for selection to improve. Darwin answers with an observation rather than an argument from principle:

> "No country can be named in which all the native inhabitants are now so perfectly adapted to each other and to the physical conditions under which they live, that none of them could anyhow be improved; for in all countries, the natives have been so far conquered by naturalised productions, that they have allowed foreigners to take firm possession of the land."

The logic runs backwards from a fact to a conclusion:

1. In every country, introduced (naturalised) species have established themselves and taken firm possession of ground.
2. To do so they must have beaten some natives in the struggle for life.
3. Therefore those natives were beatable — "we may safely conclude that the natives might have been modified with advantage, so as to have better resisted such intruders."

Perfect adaptation would have left no opening. The universal success of foreigners is the standing proof that no such perfection exists anywhere. Notice the shape of the reasoning: naturalisation is used as *evidence about the natives*, not merely as a fact about immigrants.

This dovetails with the earlier point about islands. Where a country is open on its borders, unfilled places "would have been seized on by intruders"; where barriers keep better-adapted forms out, those same places are instead filled by the modification of the original inhabitants. Immigration and modification are two ways of filling the same vacancies — which is exactly why the success of immigrants tells us the vacancies were there.

## 4. Why nature outperforms the breeder

The same section closes the comparison with man's selection, and the contrasts are worth listing because they explain why nature's productions "bear the stamp of far higher workmanship":

- Man acts only on external and visible characters; nature acts on every internal organ, every shade of constitutional difference, "the whole machinery of life."
- Man selects for his own good; nature only for the good of the being she tends.
- Man keeps the natives of many climates in one country, feeds a long- and a short-beaked pigeon the same food, exposes long- and short-woolled sheep to the same climate; nature places each being under well-suited conditions and fully exercises every selected character.
- Man does not let the most vigorous males struggle for the females, and protects his inferior animals rather than rigidly destroying them.
- Man often begins from some half-monstrous form, or at least a modification prominent enough to catch his eye; under nature "the slightest difference of structure or constitution may well turn the nicely-balanced scale."

And above all: "How fleeting are the wishes and efforts of man! how short his time!" Time is the recurring theme of this lesson. Little variations, no crisis required, an imperfectly adapted world everywhere — given geological ages, that is enough.

## Summary

| Claim | Darwin's grounds |
|---|---|
| Changed conditions increase variability | They act specially on the reproductive system |
| Extreme variability is unnecessary | Man gets great results from mere individual differences; nature has incomparably longer time |
| Great physical change or isolation is unnecessary | Inhabitants struggle with nicely balanced forces; slight modifications tip the scale and compound |
| No natives are perfectly adapted | Everywhere foreigners have taken firm possession, so natives could have been modified with advantage |

lessons.title: What Man Can and Cannot Do
lessons.content:
# What Man Can and Cannot Do

By the time Darwin reaches the middle of Chapter IV, he has already argued that selection works — the pigeon fanciers and sheep breeders proved that. The question now is how nature's version of the process compares with the breeder's. Darwin's answer is a **catalogue of the breeder's handicaps**. Read as rhetoric, it is a demolition of human selection; read as argument, it is a claim that every limitation on man is precisely the thing nature does *not* suffer from.

> "As man can produce and certainly has produced a great result by his methodical and unconscious means of selection, what may not nature effect?"

Let us take the handicaps one at a time.

## 1. Man acts only on external and visible characters

The breeder can only pick what he can see. A slightly larger comb, a whiter fleece, a longer beak — these are the currency of the show bench.

> "Man can act only on external and visible characters: nature cares nothing for appearances, except in so far as they may be useful to any being. She can act on every internal organ, on every shade of constitutional difference, on the whole machinery of life."

Notice the careful phrasing: nature is not *indifferent* to appearance. She cares about appearance exactly in proportion to its usefulness to the organism — no more, no less. A colour that hides a bird from a hawk is as much her business as a liver or a lung. But she is not restricted to the surface, and this alone gives her an enormously larger field of variation to work with.

## 2. Man selects only for his own good

> "Man selects only for his own good; Nature only for that of the being which she tends."

The breeder's criterion is the breeder's profit or pleasure. Nothing guarantees that a fatter pig or a more extravagantly feathered pigeon is a *better* pig or pigeon in any other sense — and often it is plainly worse off. Nature's criterion, by contrast, is the good of the organism itself, because only organisms that do well leave descendants. This is why Darwin can say her productions are "truer" in character.

## 3. Selected characters are not exercised, and conditions are mismatched

Under nature, Darwin says, "Every selected character is fully exercised by her; and the being is placed under well-suited conditions of life." The breeder manages neither. Darwin lists his failures almost as an indictment:

- **He keeps the natives of many climates in the same country.** A farmyard may hold animals whose ancestors came from a dozen different regions, all of them now under one sky.
- **He seldom exercises each selected character in some peculiar and fitting manner.** A long-backed or long-legged quadruped is not given the work that its long back or long legs would suit it for.
- **He feeds a long-beaked and a short-beaked pigeon on the same food.** The beak is selected for, but the conditions that would make one beak better than the other are never applied.
- **He exposes sheep with long and short wool to the same climate.** Again the character is bred for and then made irrelevant by the uniform conditions.

The point is subtle and worth dwelling on. The breeder produces a difference in structure without producing the difference in circumstance that would make that structure *count for anything*. Nature never separates the two: a beak arises in the context of the food it must handle, a fleece in the context of the weather it must resist.

## 4. Man does not let the vigorous males struggle, and protects the inferior

> "He does not allow the most vigorous males to struggle for the females. He does not rigidly destroy all inferior animals, but protects during each varying season, as far as lies in his power, all his productions."

This is the sharpest contrast of all. The breeder's whole instinct is preservation — he shelters his stock through hard winters and poor seasons, saving the weak along with the strong. Nature does the opposite: any variation "in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed." Human selection is therefore leaky, letting through in every generation the very individuals that natural selection would remove.

## 5. Man starts from the conspicuous; nature from the imperceptible

> "He often begins his selection by some half-monstrous form; or at least by some modification prominent enough to catch his eye, or to be plainly useful to him. Under nature, the slightest difference of structure or constitution may well turn the nicely-balanced scale in the struggle for life, and so be preserved."

The breeder needs a difference big enough to notice. Nature has no such threshold. Because all the inhabitants of a country are "struggling together with nicely balanced forces," a difference far too small for any human eye can decide who survives.

## 6. Time

> "How fleeting are the wishes and efforts of man! how short his time!"

A fancier's fashion lasts a few decades; a breed may be abandoned when tastes change. Nature accumulates "during whole geological periods," and — as Darwin says earlier in the chapter — although extreme variability is not needed, Nature can work up mere individual differences "far more easily, from having incomparably longer time at her disposal."

## The conclusion Darwin draws

Given all this, the surprise would be if human breeds *could* match wild species:

> "Can we wonder, then, that nature's productions should be far 'truer' in character than man's productions; that they should be infinitely better adapted to the most complex conditions of life, and should plainly bear the stamp of far higher workmanship?"

The rhetorical move is elegant. Domestic breeds were the sceptic's best evidence that selection produces only limited, superficial change. Darwin agrees that domestic breeds are limited — and then shows that every one of those limits is a feature of the *breeder*, not of *selection*. Remove the breeder's blindness, his self-interest, his uniform conditions, his mercy, and his short life, and there is no reason left to expect the results to stay small.

## A caution about reading this passage

Darwin writes of Nature as "she," as caring, tending, scrutinising. This is metaphor, and he knows it. The substance underneath is entirely mechanical: more individuals are born than can survive, so any advantage however slight improves the chance of surviving and leaving offspring. "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection." Variations that are neither useful nor injurious, he adds, are not affected at all, and are left "a fluctuating element."

lessons.title: Nature's Advantages: Scope, Fitness, and Time
lessons.content:
# Nature's Advantages: Scope, Fitness, and Time

## The rhetorical setting

By the middle of Chapter IV Darwin has already defined natural selection — "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection" — and has argued that no country is so perfectly adapted that its natives could not be improved. He now needs to persuade a reader who accepts the power of the pigeon-fancier and the sheep-breeder that an unconscious natural process could do far more. He does it with a single rhetorical question:

> "As man can produce and certainly has produced a great result by his methodical and unconscious means of selection, what may not nature effect?"

What follows is a sustained **contrast portrait**, built clause by clause. Each sentence names something man's selection cannot do, then names nature doing it. The passage works less like an argument from evidence than like a comparison of two workmen — and the comparison is rigged, deliberately and openly, in nature's favour.

## Advantage one: scope

> "Man can act only on external and visible characters: nature cares nothing for appearances, except in so far as they may be useful to any being. She can act on every internal organ, on every shade of constitutional difference, on the whole machinery of life."

The breeder is limited by his own eyes. He selects the pigeon whose tail he can count feathers in, the sheep whose fleece he can weigh. Nature is under no such limitation: a difference in a liver, a kidney, a digestive enzyme, a tolerance for cold — any of these can decide who survives, whether or not the difference is visible to anyone. Note Darwin's careful qualification: nature is not indifferent to appearances as such, but only "except in so far as they may be useful to any being." Appearance matters to nature exactly to the degree that it affects survival — which is precisely the argument he will develop in the next paragraphs about the colours of grouse and the white pigeons that hawks pick off.

## Advantage two: purpose

> "Man selects only for his own good; Nature only for that of the being which she tends."

Human selection improves the animal *as a possession* — fatter, woollier, faster, prettier. It may make the animal worse off in itself. Nature's selection, by definition, can only preserve what benefits the possessor of the variation. Darwin repeats this constraint in the following paragraph — "natural selection can act only through and for the good of each being" — because it is a limit as well as an advantage, and he will need it later.

## Advantage three: fit between character and conditions

This is the least often quoted part of the passage and one of the sharpest.

> "Every selected character is fully exercised by her; and the being is placed under well-suited conditions of life."

Then the counter-list, each item a small indictment of the breeder:

- "Man keeps the natives of many climates in the same country"
- "he feeds a long and a short beaked pigeon on the same food"
- "he does not exercise a long-backed or long-legged quadruped in any peculiar manner"
- "he exposes sheep with long and short wool to the same climate"

The point is subtle. A long beak is only meaningfully a *better* beak in the setting where long beaks matter. Feed both pigeons the same grain and the character is never tested, so the breeder is selecting a shape rather than a working advantage. Nature never separates the character from its trial: the organism lives in the conditions that make its structure count. A structure and its circumstances are selected together.

## Advantage four: rigour

> "He does not allow the most vigorous males to struggle for the females. He does not rigidly destroy all inferior animals, but protects during each varying season, as far as lies in his power, all his productions."

The breeder is, in his own way, merciful — he shelters his stock through hard winters and pairs his animals by hand. That mercy blunts selection. In nature the culling is unremitting, and combat among males adds a second filter that the farmyard removes. Notice too Darwin's remark that man "often begins his selection by some half-monstrous form; or at least by some modification prominent enough to catch his eye." Man needs a conspicuous starting point; nature does not: "Under nature, the slightest difference of structure or constitution may well turn the nicely-balanced scale in the struggle for life, and so be preserved."

## Advantage five: time

> "How fleeting are the wishes and efforts of man! how short his time! and consequently how poor will his products be, compared with those accumulated by nature during whole geological periods."

Two distinct things are short about man: his *time* and his *wishes*. A fashion in pigeons lasts a few decades; a breeder dies and his successor wants something else. Nature's "wish" — survival — never changes and never stops. Darwin has already prepared this point earlier in the chapter: man can build up mere individual differences, "so could Nature, but far more easily, from having incomparably longer time at her disposal." And in the paragraph immediately after our passage he gives the process its most famous formulation: natural selection is "daily and hourly scrutinising, throughout the world, every variation, even the slightest ... silently and insensibly working, whenever and wherever opportunity offers."

## The conclusion, and its language

> "Can we wonder, then, that nature's productions should be far 'truer' in character than man's productions; that they should be infinitely better adapted to the most complex conditions of life, and should plainly bear the stamp of far higher workmanship?"

Three claims, escalating. *Truer in character* is a breeder's technical term — Darwin has just used it in the same sense about grouse colour, "keeping that colour, when once acquired, true and constant." A true-breeding variety throws consistent offspring; nature's varieties are truer than the fancier's. *Better adapted to the most complex conditions* is the scientific claim proper. *The stamp of far higher workmanship* is the rhetorical climax — and it is a striking phrase for Darwin to choose, since "workmanship" is the vocabulary of natural theology, of the Divine artificer. He takes the language of design and awards the compliment to an unconscious process. The whole comparison, note, is put as a question the reader is invited to answer, not as an assertion: "Can we wonder, then...?"

## What kind of argument is this?

It is worth being clear-eyed. Nothing in this passage is an observation of natural selection happening. It is an argument *a fortiori*: if the weaker workman achieves so much, the stronger must achieve more. Its persuasive force depends entirely on the reader having already granted Chapter I's evidence about the power of domestic breeding. Darwin knows this, which is why he immediately turns, in the next paragraphs, to concrete cases — green leaf-eating insects, the white winter ptarmigan, downy versus smooth-skinned fruits — where the trifling characters he claims nature can act upon are shown actually mattering.

A final caution about the personification. "She can act on every internal organ"; "Nature only for that of the being which she tends." Darwin writes nature as a discerning female breeder throughout, and the figure does real work: it makes an impersonal statistical process imaginable. But every capacity he credits to her cashes out as a fact about differential survival, not as an intention. The metaphor is a ladder, and the rest of the chapter kicks it away.

lessons.title: Silent and Insensible Work

# Silent and Insensible Work

At the close of his comparison between man's selection and nature's, Darwin gathers the whole argument of the chapter into a single sentence. It is one of the most quoted sentences he ever wrote, and it repays being read slowly, clause by clause:

> It may be said that natural selection is daily and hourly scrutinising, throughout the world, every variation, even the slightest; rejecting that which is bad, preserving and adding up all that is good; silently and insensibly working, whenever and wherever opportunity offers, at the improvement of each organic being in relation to its organic and inorganic conditions of life. We see nothing of these slow changes in progress, until the hand of time has marked the long lapse of ages, and then so imperfect is our view into long past geological ages, that we only see that the forms of life are now different from what they formerly were.

Notice first the hedge with which it opens: *it may be said*. Darwin knows he is about to personify a process that has no eyes, no intentions, and no schedule. The metaphor of a scrutiniser is offered as a way of speaking, not as a claim that nature is a watchful being.

## Daily, hourly, throughout the world

The three words do three different jobs.

- **Daily and hourly** answers *when*. Selection is not an occasional event that strikes at moments of crisis. Earlier in the chapter Darwin used a change of climate as a convenient illustration, but he was careful to add that no great physical change and no unusual isolation is actually *necessary*. Because "all the inhabitants of each country are struggling together with nicely balanced forces," extremely slight modifications can give an advantage at any time. Selection is therefore continuous, not episodic.
- **Throughout the world** answers *where*. There is no reserve of ground exempt from it. Darwin has just argued the point: no country can be named whose natives are so perfectly adapted that none of them could be improved, since in all countries naturalised foreigners have taken firm possession of some of the land.
- **Every variation, even the slightest** answers *what*. This is the boldest clause. Man, Darwin has said, "often begins his selection by some half-monstrous form; or at least by some modification prominent enough to catch his eye." Nature has no eye to catch. Under nature "the slightest difference of structure or constitution may well turn the nicely-balanced scale in the struggle for life, and so be preserved."

## Rejecting the bad, adding up the good

Two verbs, and they are not symmetrical. *Rejecting* is a single act performed on a single variation; a variation "in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed." *Adding up* is cumulative, and it is what turns a scatter of trivial differences into a structure. This is exactly the analogy with the breeder that Darwin drew earlier: man "can certainly produce great results by adding up in any given direction mere individual differences, so could Nature, but far more easily, from having incomparably longer time at her disposal."

Remember also the third category, from the definition Darwin gave a few pages earlier: variations neither useful nor injurious are not acted on at all, and are "left a fluctuating element." The scrutiny is total, but the verdict is often no verdict.

## "In relation to its… conditions of life"

Darwin does not say selection works at the improvement of each being, full stop. He says it works at improvement *in relation to its organic and inorganic conditions of life* — that is, in relation to the other living things around it (competitors, prey, predators, parasites) and to the physical setting (climate, soil, light). Improvement is always relative to a situation, and if the situation changes, what counted as improvement changes with it. There is no absolute ladder being climbed.

## Why we see nothing

*Silently and insensibly* is not decoration. It is Darwin's answer to an obvious objection: if this is happening daily and hourly everywhere, why has nobody noticed it? Because the individual steps are, by hypothesis, too small to register on any human observer within any human span. "How fleeting are the wishes and efforts of man! how short his time!"

The second sentence then closes the escape route that a reader might reach for next. Very well, we cannot watch it happen — but surely the rocks record it? Darwin's answer is a deliberate double disappointment:

1. We see nothing **until** the hand of time has marked the long lapse of ages. Only deep time makes the effect visible at all.
2. **And then** our view into those long past ages is itself so imperfect that we see only the bare fact that forms of life are now different from what they formerly were — not the gradual series by which they became different.

So the evidence from the past is real but coarse: it gives Darwin change, not the mechanism of change. The mechanism has to be argued for from what can be observed in the present.

## The scrutiny of trifles, tested

Immediately after the passage, Darwin cashes out the phrase "every variation, even the slightest" with cases that look far too petty to matter:

- Leaf-eating insects are green, bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan is white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, the black-grouse the colour of peaty earth. Grouse suffer largely from birds of prey, and hawks are guided to their prey by eyesight — so much so that in parts of the Continent people are warned not to keep white pigeons, as the likeliest to be destroyed.
- In plants, botanists treat the down on a fruit and the colour of its flesh as characters of the most trifling importance. Yet Downing, an excellent horticulturist, reports that in the United States smooth-skinned fruits suffer far more from a beetle, a curculio, than downy ones; that purple plums suffer far more from a certain disease than yellow plums; and that another disease attacks yellow-fleshed peaches more than other-coloured flesh.

Darwin adds a breeder's reminder against dismissing rare losses: in a flock of white sheep it is essential to destroy every lamb with the faintest trace of black. Small and occasional destruction, repeated, is not a small effect. If such differences already tell under cultivation "with all the aids of art," then in nature, where a tree must struggle with other trees and a host of enemies, they "would effectually settle which variety… should succeed."

That is the point of the great passage in miniature: the scrutiny is fine-grained enough to weigh the fuzz on a plum, and slow enough that we never catch it in the act.

That only organic conditions, such as competitors and predators, can drive selection

options: They are not affected by natural selection and remain a fluctuating element
They are slowly rejected, since anything without a use is eventually destroyed
They are preserved and added up along with the useful variations
They become useful in time, because conditions of life are always changing
quiz.answer: They are not affected by natural selection and remain a fluctuating element

quiz.answer: That hawks are guided to their prey by eyesight, so conspicuous colour is dangerous — which supports the claim that the tints of grouse and insects serve to preserve them from danger and could be produced and kept constant by natural selection.

lessons.title: Colour and Concealment in Animals
lessons.content:
# Colour and Concealment in Animals

## Why a mere tint matters

One of the harder things to accept about natural selection is that it works on characters we would never think worth noticing. A shade of green, a speckling of grey, the whiteness of a bird in winter — these look like decoration, not equipment. Darwin's answer in Chapter IV is direct:

> "Although natural selection can act only through and for the good of each being, yet characters and structures, which we are apt to consider as of very trifling importance, may thus be acted on."

The test he proposes is not a laboratory one. It is a pattern in nature: does the colouring of an animal match the background it lives against? If it does, over and over, in unrelated groups, then the tint is doing something.

## Darwin's roll-call of matches

He lists five cases in a single sentence, and each is a match between creature and surroundings:

| Organism | Colour | Background it lives on |
|---|---|---|
| Leaf-eating insects | green | leaves |
| Bark-feeding insects | mottled-grey | bark |
| Alpine ptarmigan | white **in winter** | snow |
| Red-grouse | the colour of heather | heather moor |
| Black-grouse | the colour of peaty earth | peat |

Notice that the ptarmigan's case carries an extra piece of evidence inside it. The bird is not simply white; it is white *in winter*. A colour that changes with the season is very hard to read as an accident, because the background it matches also changes with the season.

Notice too that red-grouse and black-grouse are close relatives living in the same general country, yet they are differently coloured — and each is coloured like the particular ground it favours. Darwin concludes: "we must believe that these tints are of service to these birds and insects in preserving them from danger."

## The danger being preserved from

A concealing colour is only useful if something is hunting you, and hunting you *by sight*. Darwin supplies both halves of that condition for grouse.

First, grouse are heavily preyed upon. They "are known to suffer largely from birds of prey," and — following the argument of the previous chapter — if they were not destroyed at some period of their lives they "would increase in countless numbers." Enormous numbers are born; most die; the deaths are not random with respect to how easily a bird is spotted.

Second, the predator uses its eyes: "hawks are guided by eyesight to their prey." Darwin does not merely assert this; he offers a piece of everyday human testimony as proof. On parts of the Continent, people are warned not to keep white pigeons, because white birds are the most liable to destruction. This is a small, homely fact from pigeon-keepers, but it does exactly the work required: it shows that a conspicuous colour, all else being equal, gets an animal killed. If that is true of a domestic pigeon in a yard, the same eyesight is operating on the moor.

From these two facts Darwin draws his conclusion: he can "see no reason to doubt that natural selection might be most effective in giving the proper colour to each kind of grouse, and in keeping that colour, when once acquired, true and constant." Selection here does two jobs — it *produces* the match, and afterwards it *maintains* it, since any bird that drifts away from the right tint is the one the hawk sees.

## "But surely one bird now and then makes no difference?"

The obvious objection is that occasional deaths of oddly coloured individuals could hardly steer a whole species. Darwin meets it with an analogy from the breeder's yard:

> "we should remember how essential it is in a flock of white sheep to destroy every lamb with the faintest trace of black."

A shepherd keeping a pure white flock knows that culling *only* the faintly off-coloured lambs is enough to keep the flock white. The removal looks trivial each year; the cumulative effect is total. Nature does the same thing to grouse, only with hawks instead of shepherds, and with far more time.

## The same logic outside animals

Darwin extends the point to characters botanists call "of the most trifling importance" — the down on a fruit's skin and the colour of its flesh. He cites the horticulturist Downing, in the United States: smooth-skinned fruits suffer far more from a beetle, a curculio, than downy ones; purple plums suffer far more from a certain disease than yellow plums; while another disease attacks yellow-fleshed peaches more than other-fleshed ones. If such differences already decide outcomes under cultivation, "with all the aids of art," then in the wild — where a tree struggles with other trees and a host of enemies — they would settle which variety succeeds.

## What to take away

1. Apparent trifles are not exempt from selection; the question is always whether they are useful to their possessor.
2. A colour that matches its usual background, especially one that shifts with the seasons, is evidence of service rather than accident.
3. The argument needs a sighted enemy, and Darwin supplies one — hawks hunting by eyesight, corroborated by the warning against white pigeons.
4. Small, occasional destruction is enough, as the white-sheep flock shows, because its effects accumulate.

lessons.title: Small Differences, Large Consequences in Plants
lessons.content:
# Small Differences, Large Consequences in Plants

## The problem with "trifling" characters

Darwin has just argued that natural selection scrutinises every variation, "rejecting that which is bad, preserving and adding up all that is good." But an obvious objection arises. Many of the characters by which naturalists distinguish varieties and species look utterly useless — the exact tint of a bird's plumage, the fuzz on a peach, the colour of the flesh inside a plum. If such characters are of no consequence to the organism, selection cannot touch them, and the theory loses much of its reach.

Darwin's response is not to deny that these characters *look* trifling. It is to show, case by case, that our judgement of what is trifling is unreliable. As he puts it:

> "Although natural selection can act only through and for the good of each being, yet characters and structures, which we are apt to consider as of very trifling importance, may thus be acted on."

He first makes the case with colour in animals: leaf-eating insects are green, bark-feeders mottled-grey, the alpine ptarmigan white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, the black-grouse the colour of peaty earth. Grouse suffer largely from birds of prey, and "hawks are guided by eyesight to their prey" — so much so that on parts of the Continent people are warned not to keep white pigeons, as being the most liable to destruction. Colour, apparently a mere appearance, is in fact a matter of life and death.

## The flock of white sheep

A sceptic might still shrug: surely the occasional destruction of one oddly coloured animal amounts to nothing over the long run? Darwin meets this with a homely analogy drawn from stock-breeding:

> "we should remember how essential it is in a flock of white sheep to destroy every lamb with the faintest trace of black."

The force of the analogy lies in the word *faintest*. Breeders who want a pure white flock do not wait for a black lamb; they cull the lamb with the barest smudge, because they know that a tiny tendency, left in the flock, is heritable and will spread. The breeder's severity is a model of what nature does automatically. If a shepherd's steady removal of slightly-off individuals is enough to hold a whole flock true in colour, then the steady removal of slightly-off individuals in nature is likewise enough to fix and keep a character "true and constant."

Notice the structure of the argument: Darwin is not claiming that a black lamb is doomed in nature. He is claiming that *small, repeated, consistent elimination* has large cumulative results — which is the whole logic of selection compressed into one sentence.

## Downing's fruit trees

Darwin then turns from animals to plants, where the objection bites hardest. "In plants the down on the fruit and the colour of the flesh are considered by botanists as characters of the most trifling importance." These are exactly the sorts of details used to tell one variety from another and dismissed as of no functional consequence.

Against this he cites Downing, "an excellent horticulturist," reporting from the United States three observations:

1. **Down on the skin.** Smooth-skinned fruits suffer far more from a beetle, a curculio, than fruits with down. The fuzz is, in effect, armour against an insect.
2. **Skin colour in plums.** Purple plums suffer far more from a certain disease than yellow plums.
3. **Flesh colour in peaches.** Another disease attacks yellow-fleshed peaches far more than peaches with other coloured flesh.

Several things are worth pausing on here. First, the evidence is *horticultural*, not theoretical — Darwin is borrowing the practical knowledge of a man whose business is growing fruit, just as elsewhere he borrows from pigeon-fanciers and stock-breeders. Second, the three cases do not all point the same way: yellow is an advantage in plums but a liability in peaches (against a different disease). There is no general virtue in being yellow or being purple. Advantage is always relative to a particular enemy under particular conditions.

## The inference to a state of nature

The final move is the important one. Downing's trees are cultivated — sprayed, pruned, tended, protected. Darwin argues that this makes the evidence *stronger*, not weaker:

> "If, with all the aids of art, these slight differences make a great difference in cultivating the several varieties, assuredly, in a state of nature, where the trees would have to struggle with other trees and with a host of enemies, such differences would effectually settle which variety, whether a smooth or downy, a yellow or purple fleshed fruit, should succeed."

The logic is *a fortiori*: if a difference shows through even under the cushioning of human care, it must weigh far more heavily where there is no cushioning at all. In the orchard, the grower can compensate for a susceptible variety. In the wild, the tree faces competing trees plus "a host of enemies" with no help whatever, and the same small difference becomes decisive.

This connects directly to Darwin's earlier contrast between man's selection and nature's. Man "does not rigidly destroy all inferior animals, but protects during each varying season, as far as lies in his power, all his productions," and he "often begins his selection by some half-monstrous form; or at least by some modification prominent enough to catch his eye." Nature is neither so protective nor so coarse-grained: "Under nature, the slightest difference of structure or constitution may well turn the nicely-balanced scale in the struggle for life, and so be preserved."

## What the section accomplishes

Darwin does not prove that fruit down or flesh colour has actually been shaped by natural selection in any wild species. What he establishes is more modest and more useful: our intuition about which characters are unimportant is worthless. A character that botanists classify as "of the most trifling importance" turns out, on the testimony of someone who actually grows the plants, to govern which variety survives an infestation. Once that intuition is discredited, the objection that selection cannot explain small differences loses its footing.

Downy fruits attract the beetle, which lays its eggs among the hairs
The beetle avoids both downy and smooth fruit, preferring the flesh colour
Down makes no difference to the beetle, but protects the fruit from disease

The same disease spares them entirely, as it spares the yellow plums
They resist that disease but are more heavily attacked by the curculio
Their flesh colour has no recorded effect, unlike their skin colour

quiz.question: What point is Darwin making with the remark that in a flock of white sheep it is essential to destroy every lamb with the faintest trace of black?

That black lambs are inherently weaker and would perish in nature without the shepherd's help
That breeders, unlike nature, are able to select for internal constitution as well as colour
That colour variations arise so rarely in domestic flocks that each one must be seized upon
quiz.answer: That the repeated elimination of even slightly deviant individuals produces large cumulative results
